spec.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. In particular E is constant on (0,∞). No assertion at time zero is made.

definitions.definition: u_t(x,t)=∂u(x,t)/∂t, component by component. Derivatives are the usual real derivatives; a derivative not existing is assigned the total derivative convention value zero. When u is smooth on its open domain these are classical derivatives.
u_tt(x,t)=∂u_t(x,t)/∂t, component by component, with the same total derivative convention.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u(x,t), the derivative along the jth standard coordinate direction, component by component with the total derivative convention. We also write u_j when the index j is explicitly fixed.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_jj(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_j(j,x,t), with the total derivative convention. The notation u_jj with fixed j has this same meaning.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: v_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t), with the total derivative convention. With fixed j we abbreviate this by v_j.
Δu(x,t)=∑_{j=1}^n u_jj(j,x,t), the componentwise spatial Laplacian Δ_xu of the input.

e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |u_j(j,x,t)|². Here |z|²=z·z is the Euclidean norm square on ℝ^m, so the spatial sum is exactly the Frobenius square |Du|². All integrals in the proof are Lebesgue integrals, and dx denotes standard volume on ℝ^n.
e_t(x,t)=∂e(x,t)/∂t, using the total derivative convention, whose classical existence and formula will be proved.
For t>0, E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx. This finite Lebesgue integral is used only once integrability of e(·,t) at every positive time has been proved; no definition at time zero is required.

propositions.statement: n≥1 and m≥1. The map u and all its partial derivatives are smooth on ℝ^n×(0,∞); in particular ∂_t u_j(j,x,t)=v_j(j,x,t) and e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2∑_{j=1}^n u_j(j,x,t)·v_j(j,x,t). For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊆ℝ^n and R>0 such that C⊆(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and every positive-order derivative of u vanishes for x∉C and r∈int J. Put Q=[−R,R]^n, whose Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n. For every r∈int J the following scalar spatial functions are continuous, zero outside C, and Lebesgue integrable: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j, u_j(j,·,r)·v_j(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_jj(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r)). Their absolute integrals are finite, each bounded by a finite supremum on Q times (2R)^n. In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary spatial point x.
Choose a scalar a given by H005 at (x,t), so u_tt(x,t)−Δu(x,t)=a u(x,t).
For the spatial second-derivative identity, fix any j∈{1,…,n}.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary x∈ℝ^n and t>0. H004 gives u·u=1 on the whole domain. The time section is differentiable near t by H002. Applying M006 with both functions equal to this section gives 0=∂_t(u·u)=2u·u_t, hence u·u_t=0. Whenever a source is formulated for a function on all of ℝ, a time section may be set to zero for nonpositive times; it agrees with the given section on a neighborhood of t, so its derivative at t is unchanged. This convention is only for applying sources and does not define u at time zero.

produces.statement: For every spatial point y∈ℝ^n and every positive time r, u(y,r)·u_t(y,r)=0.

argument.text: Choose a from H005 at (x,t). Dot its identity with u_t. F001 at (x,t) and symmetry of the Euclidean dot product give u_t·(u_tt−Δu)=a(u_t·u)=0. Only this pointwise choice is used; a is never differentiated.

Retain also the supplied explicit equation calculation. Since F001 is an identity on an open time interval, M006 applied to the time sections of u and u_t gives 0=∂_t(u·u_t)=|u_t|²+u·u_tt, so u·u_tt=−|u_t|². For any fixed j, apply M006 first to u with itself along a spatial coordinate line, obtaining u·u_j=0 from H004, and then to u and u_j along that line, obtaining u·u_jj=−|u_j|². All sections and their derivatives are differentiable by H002. Dot the equation defining a with u. Since u·u=1, a=u·u_tt−∑_j u·u_jj=∑_j|u_j|²−|u_t|². The last computation works for every scalar satisfying the normality equation, and does not give it any assumed regularity. Together with F001 and F002, universal introduction in x,t and the arbitrary spatial index proves N001.

argument.text: H001 supplies n,m≥1. Fix t0>0 and J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. The endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2, so H006 gives a compact spatial set common to all times in J. Separately, H002 ensures that all partial derivatives of u are smooth on the open domain. M007 over ℝ at each point, applied to the spatial and time coordinate vectors, gives ∂_t u_j=v_j. The input is locally smooth at that point, so it is in particular C² there; if a total ambient map is needed, extend u by zero off the positive-time domain, which leaves it smooth on a neighborhood of the point. Differentiating each squared norm using M006, and the finite-sum differentiation rule, therefore gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_j u_j·v_j throughout the domain. These formulas also show e and e_t are smooth.

produces.statement: There exists a compact C0⊆ℝ^n such that u(y,r)=q for every y∉C0 and r∈J.
All partial derivatives of u are smooth on the open positive-time domain; ∂_t u_j=v_j and e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n u_j·v_j at every point. The functions e and e_t are smooth there.

argument.text: Choose C from F001. Apply M008 on C to the identity map into Euclidean ℝ^n. It gives a finite real bound on |x| for x∈C. Increase this bound, if necessary, to a positive R larger than it. Since |x_j|≤|x|, C⊆(−R,R)^n. Thus such a positive R exists, even if C is empty.

produces.statement: There exists R0>0 such that C⊆(−R0,R0)^n.

argument.text: Choose R from F002 and set Q=[−R,R]^n. This closed box is compact, measurable, and has finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n. The compact set C is closed in ℝ^n. On the open set (ℝ^n\C)×int J, F001 says u=q. At every point of this open set u is constant in a neighborhood; differentiating the constant on that neighborhood, successively in each coordinate, gives zero for every positive-order derivative. Consequently at any r∈int J all the functions listed in N002 vanish outside C: every summand contains such a derivative. For the last function, the product rule expands it into v_j·u_j+u_t·u_jj, both of which vanish there. Continuity and smoothness follow from F003 and smoothness of the dot product.

produces.statement: C⊆int Q, and Q is compact and measurable with finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n. For every r∈int J, the spatial functions e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for every j∈{1,…,n}, u_j(j,·,r)·v_j(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_jj(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r)) are continuous and vanish outside C. Their nonzero sets therefore have closures contained in the compact set C.

argument.text: For every r∈int J apply M005 to each continuous scalar function in F004, on ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure. Its support closure is a closed subset of compact C, hence compact; Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets. Each is therefore integrable. Equivalently its norm is bounded on Q by M008 and it vanishes outside Q, so its absolute integral is at most that finite bound times |Q|=(2R)^n. This also supplies the stated finiteness estimate for all terms. Since t0 belongs to int J, e(·,t0) is integrable. As t0 was arbitrary, this holds at every positive time. Together with F003 and F004 this proves the complete statement N002, including the common support witnesses and all derivative-product integrability assertions.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and choose C,R from N002. Put Q=[−R,R]^n, η=t0/4 and I=[t0−η,t0+η]. The elementary endpoint inequalities place I strictly inside (t0/2,3t0/2). N002 makes E a finite integral at every positive time, so its guarded definition is now available. Its density and e_t are continuous on the compact set Q×I. M008 applied there to e_t gives a finite bound; replacing it by its maximum with zero gives a B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B on Q×I.

produces.statement: There exists B0≥0 such that |e_t(x,r)|≤B0 for every x∈Q and r∈I.

argument.text: Choose B as in F001 and define F and b as in the local declarations. For any x∈Q, the scalar time section r↦e(x,r) is differentiable on I by N002, with derivative e_t(x,r). Apply M002 on the convex interval I, with derivative the linear map multiplying by e_t(x,r), whose operator norm is |e_t(x,r)|≤B. For 0<|h|<η both t0 and t0+h lie in I, so |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|. Division by |h| gives |F(h)(x)|≤B. Outside Q, N002 gives both densities zero, since both times lie inside the common time slab. Hence |F(h)(x)|≤b(x) on all of ℝ^n. The function b is integrable: Q is measurable of finite measure (2R)^n and ∫|b|=B(2R)^n<∞. For each such h, F(h) is continuous and integrable, by N002's integrability at its two times and linearity. At each x, the definition of e_t as the classical derivative gives F(h)(x)→e_t(x,t0) as h→0 through nonzero values.

produces.statement: b is Lebesgue integrable; for all real h with 0<|h|<η, F(h) is continuous and integrable and |F(h)(x)|≤b(x) for every x∈ℝ^n. For every x∈ℝ^n, F(h)(x) tends to e_t(x,t0) as h→0 through h≠0.

argument.text: Use M001 with parameter filter the punctured neighborhood filter h→0, functions F(h), limit e_t(·,t0), and bound b. This filter is countably generated: the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k, with positive integer k, form a countable neighborhood basis. F002 supplies continuity, hence a.e. strong measurability, eventually, the everywhere dominating bound, integrability of b, and pointwise convergence. Therefore ∫F(h)→∫e_t(·,t0). For 0<|h|<η, the integrability assertions of N002 give by linearity ∫F(h)=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. The limit is exactly the derivative criterion for E at the interior time t0, so E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0) dx. This is the derivative of the actual finite energy, not just a formal integral expression. Arbitrary t0 proves N003.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and j∈{1,…,n}; N002 gives n≥1 and the compact set C, radius R>0, and Q=[−R,R]^n. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·u_j(j,x,t0) and d=∂_{x_j}g. They are smooth by N002. Apply M006 along the jth spatial coordinate line to the sections of u_t and u_j. The product rule gives d=v_j·u_j+u_t·u_jj. N002 states integrability of d and of its two summands, and also g=0 outside C. Since C⊆int Q, g vanishes on an open neighborhood of the boundary of Q, in particular at each pair of opposite j-coordinate faces.

produces.statement: d(x)=v_j(j,x,t0)·u_j(j,x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·u_jj(j,x,t0). The three scalar functions in this equality are continuous, integrable, and zero outside C. The function g is smooth and zero off C⊆int Q, so it vanishes at the j-coordinate endpoints ±R for every choice of the remaining coordinates.

argument.text: Define the insertion map ι. Fix arbitrary remaining coordinates y∈ℝ^(n−1). The function z↦g(ι(z,y)) is smooth on ℝ and its derivative is z↦d(ι(z,y)). The derivative is continuous on [−R,R], hence interval-integrable there. Apply M003 with endpoints −R,R: ∫_{−R}^R d(ι(z,y)) dz=g(ι(R,y))−g(ι(−R,y))=0 by F001. These sections of d vanish when |z|>R. Thus their full real integrals equal the interval integrals and are zero. The oriented interval integral here equals the Lebesgue integral on [−R,R], since −R<R and the two endpoints have measure zero. This argument holds for every y; when n=1 there are no remaining coordinates and ℝ^0 is a one-point product with total measure one.

produces.statement: For every y0∈ℝ^(n−1), the section z↦d(ι(z,y0)) is integrable on ℝ and ∫_ℝ d(ι(z,y0)) dz=0.

argument.text: Under the coordinate extraction inverse to ι, M009 identifies Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure on ℝ times the product measure on ℝ^(n−1). Use k=n−1, each coordinate space ℝ, and index j−1 in Fin n; n≥1 makes n=(n−1)+1. Hence the integrable function d from F001 has the same integral and integrability as (z,y)↦d(ι(z,y)) on the product. Apply M010 to that product function; its integral is ∫_{ℝ^(n−1)}(∫_ℝ d(ι(z,y)) dz)dy=0 by F002. Equivalently this is the supplied Fubini calculation over Q, since every term is zero outside Q and all terms are absolutely integrable. In particular ∫d=0. By F001 and linearity for integrable functions, 0=∫v_j·u_j+∫u_t·u_jj. Symmetry of the real dot product and rearrangement give ∫u_j·v_j=−∫u_t·u_jj, with all integrals finite. Arbitrary t0 and j yield N004.

locals.declaration: Fix arbitrary t0>0 for the derivative computation.
Define f(r)=E(r) for r>0 and f(r)=0 for r≤0.

argument.text:
Fix t0>0. N002 already proves integrability of e at every positive time and supplies the definition guard for E, as well as integrability of every term in the following calculation. N003 supplies the derivative of the finite energy. Substitute the density formula from N002 and then N004 for each spatial index. By linearity and finite summation,
E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx
=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n∫u_j·v_j dx
=2∫u_t·u_tt dx−2∑_{j=1}^n∫u_t·u_jj dx
=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δu) dx=0.
The penultimate equality uses the definition Δu=∑_j u_jj and bilinearity of the dot product. The last integrand is zero at every point by N001, so its integral is zero. This retains the factor two and the energy normalization without inserting a half. Since t0 was arbitrary, E is differentiable with zero derivative at every positive time.

produces.statement: For every r>0, E is differentiable at r and E'(r)=0.

argument.text: For completeness retain the supplied constancy consequence. Fix arbitrary s,t>0 and define the zero extension f of E as declared. On the closed interval with endpoints s,t, all times are positive. F001 says f is differentiable there with derivative zero; locality justifies use of the extension. Apply M002 with V=K=W=ℝ, this convex interval, c=0, and L identically zero. It gives |E(t)−E(s)|≤0·|t−s|=0, so E(t)=E(s), including the case s=t. Thus E is constant on (0,∞). Together with N002's integrability and F001 this proves P; no endpoint t=0 was used or asserted.
